explanations.explanation: That's the very first thing out of the LORD's mouth: "Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!" A shepherd's whole job is keeping the flock together and safe. These shepherds did the exact opposite. That's like a mail carrier tossing your letters into the bushes and calling it a route.

Nobody in this verse is running a clearance sale, friend. The LORD says the shepherds "destroy and scatter" the sheep. Selling is neat and organized, and scattering is the opposite of that. The text doesn't mention a market at all.

A pen would at least keep the flock in one place, and that's the opposite of the trouble here. The LORD says these shepherds "destroy and scatter" the sheep of His pasture. Scattered means spread out, not shut in. The verse says nothing about pens, so I'd say you were picturing a tidier problem than the one the LORD describes.

Close, but listen to how the LORD says it: "the sheep of My pasture." Then in verse 2 He says "My flock" and "My people." So the flock belongs to Him, not to the shepherds. They were only put in charge of looking after them.

That's right, baker. The LORD says "the sheep of My pasture" in verse 1, and in verse 2 He calls them "My flock" and "My people." The sheep are His. The shepherds were only tending what belonged to Him. That makes scattering them even worse, like me dropping a customer's cookie box on the floor and saying, "Oh, it's fine, it's basically mine."

You caught the turnaround. The LORD says to the shepherds, "Behold, I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds." They skipped attending to His flock, and now they're the ones getting attended to. Same word, very different delivery. Some attention you just don't want.
The nations don't come up in this verse. The LORD is speaking "about the shepherds who tend My people." And He says, "I will attend to you," so He's talking straight to those shepherds.

The sheep do get attention, but it comes in the next verse. Here the LORD says to the shepherds, "I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds." The shepherds are the ones He's talking to. For the flock, hang on, because verse 3 has good news.

He doesn't hand this job to anybody else. The LORD says, "Then I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them." The word is "Myself." The One who owns the flock goes out and gathers it.

Those are the shepherds who just heard "Woe" in verse 1, so they're not getting the rescue job. The LORD says, "I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock." Sending the scatterers to collect the flock would be like asking me to find the cookies I flung out the back door. I'd just come back with a crumb and a story.

Egypt does show up in this passage, but only in verse 7, as the land the LORD brought the Israelites up out of. Nowhere does the text give Egypt's king the gathering job. In verse 3 the LORD says, "I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock."

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "I will return them to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply." He doesn't stop at gathering. He brings them all the way home to their pasture. That's the whole trip, start to finish.

The LORD actually says the opposite. After He gathers the remnant, He says, "I will return them to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply." The gathering is only half of it. The other half is bringing them home to the pasture.

Straight from the LORD in verse 4: "I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them." The job doesn't go away. He puts new shepherds in who will actually tend. Shepherds were never the problem. Bad shepherding was.

Prophets are a fair guess, since the passage is full of the LORD's words. But the verse says something else. The LORD says, "I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them." What these sheep need is tending.
Soldiers sound strong, but they're not in this verse. The LORD says He'll raise up "shepherds over them who will tend them." The word is tend, and that's a different job from guarding.

I get why you'd pick it, friend, because I lose things in my own bakery all the time. But the LORD says that under these shepherds they "will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing." That's "nor will any," and not even a few. Not a single sheep goes missing.

You've got it. The LORD says the flock "will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing." Not a few and not one. I once lost a spatula in a bakery the size of one cookie planet, so a flock with zero missing sounds like a miracle to me.

The LORD says, "I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King." David was Israel's king, and this Branch is raised up for him. So the Branch isn't a shepherd who gets scattered or lost. He's a King who reigns wisely.

Prophets were all over Jeremiah's day, but that's not the word here. The LORD says the righteous Branch "will reign wisely as King." And the Branch is raised up for David, Israel's king. Reigning is a king's work.

Priest is a real job in Israel, but it's not the one the LORD names here. He says the righteous Branch "will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land." The Branch is raised up for David, Israel's king. So the word is King.
Yes! The LORD says, "In His days Judah will be saved." That's the word, plain and simple. It's the first half of the promise about what happens when the righteous Branch reigns.
That's the other half. The LORD says "Israel will dwell securely." Think of the flock earlier, scattered and afraid. Now they're settled in and safe.
Rebuilt sounds like a nice promise, but it's not the word the LORD uses. He says, "In His days Judah will be saved." Nothing in these verses mentions rebuilding. So the first blank is saved.
Humbled is not what the LORD says here. He says, "In His days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely." This verse is a promise of rescue. Humbled doesn't fit that, friend.

Apart is closer to the old trouble than to the promise. The sheep were scattered, and in the Branch's days the LORD says Israel "will dwell securely." So the word for the second blank is securely. Nobody is left apart in that picture.

That's the name. The LORD says, "this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." It comes right after the promise that Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell securely. Take it in slowly, because this is a name worth sitting with.

Shepherd makes sense, since the whole passage is about shepherds and sheep. But the name the LORD gives is a different one: "The LORD Our Righteousness." It's in verse 6, right after the promise of salvation and security.

Strength is a good word, but it's not the name here. The LORD says, "this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." The text gives the exact name, and the last word is Righteousness.

explanations.answer: Bringing them back from the north
explanations.explanation: That's the new line. The people will say, "As surely as the LORD lives, who brought and led the descendants of the house of Israel up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them." The old words about Egypt stay true, but this new rescue is the one they'll name. And it covers every land where He banished them, not only the north.

The Jordan never comes up in these verses. The new words in verse 8 are about the LORD bringing them "up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them." That's the rescue they'll name.

The wilderness isn't mentioned in this passage. What the people will say instead is "As surely as the LORD lives, who brought and led the descendants of the house of Israel up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them." So the answer is bringing them back from the north.
